transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (ZenithTech, Staff ML Eng), Tomás Rivera (ZenithTech, Infra Lead), Ava Kim (ZenithTech, CTO)

Summary (auto): technical deep dive on GPU runtime profiling, kernel selection, TRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs, batching and KV cache.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna dig into the GPU profiling data, priya and marcus will lead the technical part. quick run through agenda?
[00:15] Ava: thanks y'all, we care about p99 latency with a 512-token context, throughput for batch size 8, and cost — would like a side-by-side of TRT-LLM and vLLM on our model.
[00:30] Priya: got it, and also we want to show CUDA graphs impact on kernel launch overhead, plus how prefix/KV caching saves tokens across long-lived sessions.
[00:45] Marcus: quick note, our slides include trace samples captured with nvprof and a small tracer, there may be mismatches in symbol names, hope that's ok.
[01:05] Lena: that's fine, you'll probably mis-transcribe some names, ha. also we run a BPE tokenizer and our sequences are noisy — lots of short and occasional long queries.

[03:20] Priya: ok jumping in — first: kernel selection. on NVIDIA Ampere/Blackwell we see major diffs based on kernel choice: flash attention vs math-optimized matmul kernels; TRT-LLM picks fused kernels in TensorRT that combine QKV/project and attention, vLLM relies on highly-optimized linear ops + scheduling and its own flash attention when available. the real gap often comes from how kernels handle kv-cache reuse and when they can avoid re-materializing big tensors.
[03:50] Tomás: can you clarify re-materializing? like do kernels re-run some ops per step?
[04:05] Priya: yes, if the runtime doesn't support persistent KV cache or has to copy from host/other memory, you pay both memcpy and extra kernel launches. TRT-LLM when configured with CUDA graphs and persistent tensors can keep the KV cache resident and reduce launches. vLLM's scheduler reduces host roundtrips via batching and pipelining, so at short sequence lengths it can outperform naive TRT setups unless TRT uses CUDA graphs.

[07:10] Marcus: we ran a head-to-head with ZenithTech's medium LLM (1.8B-ish) on p4d-style GPUs — numbers: baseline vLLM avg latency for single request (~512 ctx) ~210ms p50, p99 ~520ms when single-threaded but with continuous batching we got throughput boosts. TRT-LLM FP16 with int8 calibration gave p50 ~160ms and p99 ~370ms in our test cluster when using CUDA graphs and cuBLAS/TensorRT fused kernels.
[07:50] Lena: interesting — did you run TRT int8 PTQ or QAT? we care about quality drop.
[08:05] Priya: this was post-training static int8 (PTQ) with per-channel scales; quality drop was small on your eval prompts — delta of ~0.8 percentage points on our accuracy metric. if you need QAT we can recommend a flow but it adds complexity.

[10:30] Jordan: a frequent question is batching window vs latency SLO — can you summarize tradeoffs?
[10:40] Marcus: sure. there's a sliding batching window: larger windows increase batching efficiency but hurt tail latency. vLLM's continuous batching tries to balance by grouping requests and service-level policies; Redwood's runtime offers smart routing by latency target so you can route small-latency traffic to a low-batch lane and background traffic to high-throughput pools. In TRT case, because CUDA graphs reduce per-step overhead, you can afford slightly larger batches without jumping p99 as much.

[13:55] Tomás: how do CUDA graphs actually help here? we assumed it was only for static graphs, and our workload has variability.
[14:10] Priya: good point — CUDA graphs capture a sequence of CUDA launches and can replay them with near-zero launch overhead. For autoregressive inference where the compute pattern repeats per token, capturing the token-step graph is beneficial. The limitation is graph re-creation cost if you change sequence length or model shape; so we use a family of graphs for common seq lengths (32/128/512) and fallback to dynamic path for others. This hybrid approach reduces overhead for the 80% common cases.

[17:00] Lena: any gotchas with dynamic batching + CUDA graphs?
[17:15] Marcus: yes — if the batching strategy changes tensor shapes (e.g., padding strategy) you may need more graph variants or extra kernel calls to pad/reshape which reduces gains. Also, for int8 we had to include calibration steps so that fused TensorRT kernels remained numerically stable.

[19:30] Priya: on KV cache — Redwood recommends prefix caching for session-heavy workloads. If you keep KV cache in-GPU and leverage persistent device memory, you avoid large host-device transfers. We profile cache hit rates: with 70% prefix reuse we saw 2.2x throughput improvement vs cold start. But you need memory headroom; for long contexts NV memory can become a constraint so quantized KV storage (e.g., FP16 or 8-bit) is used.
[20:10] Tomás: does quantized KV hurt model quality?
[20:25] Priya: small effect. We typically keep activations in FP16 and store KV in FP16 or 8-bit where acceptable. For some decoder-only models 4-bit bucketing for KV is workable but requires end-to-end eval. We'll run your sample prompts in the PI to measure quality delta.

[22:50] Jordan: customer asked about kernel selection automation. can the runtime auto-select kernels based on model and seq distribution?
[23:03] Marcus: yes, Redwood's compilation layer profiles short warmup traces and picks kernel recipes: it considers sequence length dist, hardware, and target latency to choose fused vs unfused kernels, whether to enable CUDA graphs, and quantization profile. we can expose those heuristics or let it run in an automated optimize pass.

[25:40] Ava: for private deployments / VPC we need to know what bits run in our VPC and what touches Redwood control plane; also KMS/HSM.
[25:55] Priya: Private deployment: control plane can be customer-hosted or use Redwood's minimal control plane with an on-prem agent. Model weights and inferences can stay within your VPC; only metadata for billing/health needs to be sent unless you opt for fully air-gapped. KMS integration supports customer-managed keys (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or HSM). We'll put the security doc in the artifact links.

[28:20] Lena: network egress is a concern, also multi-tenant GPU pools in dedicated vs private?
[28:35] Marcus: Dedicated reserved GPU pools are single-tenant at the node level; Redwood's networking can be configured with private IPs and no public egress. For on-prem you run the runtime inside your cluster. The main infra work is ensuring drivers, CUDA, and MIG (if using) are configured similarly to our perf benches — mismatch causes surprising slowdowns.

[31:10] Priya: back to TRT vs vLLM: short summary — TRT-LLM excels when you can compile and pin a small set of kernels, use CUDA graphs, and accept extra compile time. vLLM's strength is in scheduling, memory efficiency for very large models, and dynamic batching/prefix reuse without extensive fusing. In practice, for ZenithTech's 1.8B model we saw TRT with int8 + graphs best for single-node throughput and lower cost per token; vLLM had easier scaling across heterogeneous clusters and more graceful tail behavior for unpredictable sequences.

[34:45] Tomás: what about kernel-level instrumentation we can run ourselves?
[35:00] Marcus: we'll share scripts: nvprof/nvtx spans, CUPTI traces, TensorRT profiler snippets, and a small Redwood tracer that aggregates kernel times and memcpy. note that CUPTI has overhead and can distort micro-latency; we usually run sampling + targeted CUPTI for hotspots.

[36:40] Lena: you mentioned fused QKV kernels — are those stable across model variants? we swap heads sometimes.
[36:55] Priya: fused kernels require matching operator shapes; when you change head count or hidden dims you need to recompile. For teams that frequently change architectures we recommend a hybrid approach: keep some general kernels and fallback to vLLM-like paths, or automate recompilation in CI.

[39:15] Jordan: quality vs quantization — do we have a threshold recommendation?
[39:28] Marcus: metric driven: if your eval drop is <1% on critical metrics, int8 PTQ is often acceptable for production. If you need <0.2% drop, do QAT or keep FP16. We'll run ZenithTech's prompts and return exact deltas.

[41:50] Priya: small demo — we pulled a short nvprof trace (shared link in chat). showing kernel timeline: note the large gaps caused by cudaLaunch overhead before using CUDA graphs; with graphs launch overhead nearly disappears and time is dominated by actual GEMM/attention kernels. this is most visible at 1-2 token steps where launch overhead is a large fraction.

[44:20] Ava: are there licensing or IP issues with TensorRT-LLM?
[44:30] Jordan: TRT is NVIDIA tech; you need proper drivers and TensorRT runtime on your nodes. Redwood's Dedicated or Private offering can include those as part of the managed stack; we can detail licensing in the security/compliance doc.

[46:05] Tomás: what about multi-GPU KV cache? we plan to shard context across multiple GPUs for long contexts.
[46:20] Marcus: sharded KV needs careful kernel routing and inter-GPU comms. NCCL all-gather/peer-to-peer becomes the bottleneck if you do per-token exchange. For long contexts you can partition by layer blocks and aggregate outputs less frequently; Redwood runtime supports several sharding strategies and we can run a pilot to see which hits your latency SLOs.

[48:50] Priya: recap of recommended immediate steps: 1) run TRT-LLM int8 + CUDA graphs on a dedicated node for your 512-token workload, 2) run vLLM baseline with continuous batching and prefix caching, 3) compare p50/p99/cost and quality metrics on your prompt set.

[50:10] Lena: yes please — we'll share a small eval set and the model weights (s3 link) and Tomás will share VPC/KMS notes.
[50:25] Jordan: perfect. Action items in chat. we'll send a perf template and sample scripts; priya and marcus will own the bench runs.

[51:00] Ava: thanks team, good deep dive. we'll aim to start pilot early May.
[51:20] Jordan: thanks everyone, end.
